# Output Artifacts

Read this at Phase 9, before writing anything.

## Where artifacts go

**Nothing here has a hardcoded path.** The destination comes from the project, and Phase 2 already worked it out: whatever its scans found — ADRs, a lexicon, an assumptions record — establishes where this project keeps design documentation. Write the durable artifacts alongside it; write the feature's brief where the project's conventions say the build reads it (see *Which artifacts this design needs*).

If the scans found nothing and no documentation directory is obvious, ask. Once, in one line, **with a concrete suggestion** — one that fits what the repo actually looks like, its ecosystem's convention or a `docs/` that already exists, rather than a preference of your own. Use the answer for everything in this capture.

Ask at most once per project. After this, the files exist and Phase 2's scan finds them, so the destination is derived rather than asked.

Keep the artifacts together, and keep their names recognizable, because the next interview's scan has to find them.

## Provenance

Artifacts need detail the design tree does not always carry. The tree records decisions; a functional spec records behavior, a data model records constraints, acceptance criteria record cases. Some of that was decided in the interview. Some of it will be you filling gaps.

Both are acceptable. Only one is acceptable *silently*.

- A statement tracing to a branch closed **decided** is written plainly.
- A statement you inferred is **marked as inference, inline, with what it was inferred from.** Not collected in a footnote at the end where it reads as afterthought.
- A statement that would resolve a branch closed **deferred**, **blocked**, or **stable-open** is not written at all. Those are open on purpose, and quietly closing one in prose destroys the reason they were left open.

Never let the two look alike. A document where agreed decisions and plausible invention are typographically identical gets implemented as though all of it was agreed.

## Capture is a completeness check

Anything an artifact needs that the tree doesn't have is a gap in the interview, not a gap in your writing. Treat it that way.

When a section can't be written from decided branches:

1. Name the branches that are missing, or that closed too loosely to write from.
2. Offer to reopen them. This is a normal continuation of Phase 5 and the four locks still apply.
3. Write the section on marked inference only if the user declines.

Reaching the end of capture with no gaps to report is real evidence the interview was thorough. Reaching it having invented a third of the content and said nothing is the failure this phase exists to prevent. **Report the gap count even when it is zero.**

## Vocabulary

Every artifact uses the lexicon, and only the lexicon, for anything the lexicon names. Artifacts diverging on terminology is the specific failure the lexicon exists to prevent, and it shows up here first — the data model calling something a `member` while the contract calls it a `user` is how two correct-looking documents produce two different systems.

A term the artifacts need that isn't in the lexicon is a gap like any other. Surface it; don't quietly coin one.

**Write the lexicon back.** Whenever capture runs, the consolidated lexicon is written back to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above if there wasn't one. This is unconditional and it is not optional: the artifacts are written in this vocabulary, so a reader without the lexicon has documents whose terms mean whatever they assume. It is also what the next interview ingests. Show which entries are new and which changed before writing. An inherited entry changes only where this design changed what the word means.

## Assumptions and tracker candidates

**Write the assumptions record back**, to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above. Unconditional, like the lexicon, and for the same reason: it is not a deliverable, it is what the next interview reads, and what a review of the build checks its platform assumptions against.

It holds the assumptions still standing, each with a stable id, the assumption in one line, the subject area, and **how you would know it stopped holding** — an assumption recorded without that is decoration; with it, a later interview can actually check — plus the facts the project has measured that would cost time to rediscover. Remove an assumption the interview invalidated rather than annotating it; if the resolution was a real fork it became an ADR, and that is where the history belongs.

**Branches closed *deferred-later*, *blocked*, or *stable-open* are not written to a file.** They are the next design questions, and a file of them turns into a backlog the tracker already is. Emit them as tracker candidates: one line each with the question, why it is open, and **what would resolve it**, for the user to file. The next interview asks which tracker items touch its work.

## Which artifacts this design needs

**Two outlive the feature: the decision records and the lexicon** (and the assumptions record, above). They are kept in the tree and kept true. Everything else in the tables below is **the feature's brief**: it tells the build and its reviewers what was decided, in the detail the tree does not carry, and it is spent when the feature ships — the code is its own domain model and interface contract, the tests carry the criteria, the project's references carry the behaviour. Write the brief where the project's conventions say the build reads it: on the tracker issue when the project works from one, else in the documentation directory marked as a brief. Do not carry a brief into the next interview as if it described the system; scan the code and the durable three instead.

Four are unconditional:

| Artifact | Template |
|---|---|
| Decision records (ADRs) | the `design:adr` skill — see below |
| Functional specification | `artifacts/functional-spec.md` |
| Edge cases and error handling | `artifacts/edge-cases.md` |
| Acceptance criteria | `artifacts/acceptance-criteria.md` |

The rest are selected by the same conditions check that seeded the tree (`conditions-and-patterns.md`). If the condition held at seeding, the artifact is required now:

| Artifact | Required when | Template |
|---|---|---|
| Interface / contract definitions | *Callers you can't change in lockstep*, or any boundary between components that ship or evolve separately | `artifacts/interface-contract.md` |
| Domain model | *The same concept has more than one shape*, *state outlives a single version*, *holds data that belongs to someone else* | `artifacts/domain-model.md` |
| Non-functional requirements | *It runs inside a constrained envelope*, *someone operates it in production* | not yet templated |

There is deliberately no state-machine artifact. State and lifecycle content is unconditional and lives in the functional spec, which already requires every state, every transition, and every terminal state. A separate artifact would reformat content another artifact owns — a pass-through layer. Where a lifecycle is complex enough to need a diagram, the spec renders it as one.

### Decision records

**Every ADR-worthy decision gets an ADR, always.** Not conditional, not on request, not deferred to the user's judgment at write-up time. Invoke the `design:adr` skill and let it write them — it owns format, house rules, numbering, indexing, and supersession, and none of that is reimplemented here.

A branch that closed *decided* is ADR-worthy when a real fork existed and the decision passes the `design:adr` skill's tests for what gets an ADR. A real fork means the closure recorded it as one, with the alternatives and why each was rejected. Read that line; don't reconstruct it from the rationale. A closure recorded as *no fork* is not an ADR no matter how consequential it feels — nothing was chosen.

Not ADR-worthy: decisions with only one option ever available, choices forced by an existing constraint, anything the design-vs-implementation gate would have deferred, and anything an indexed ADR already covers.

Two cases need care:

- **A decision that contradicts an ADR indexed in Phase 2** is a supersession, not a new record. Say so and hand the `design:adr` skill both — it owns what happens next.
- **A branch that closed *stable-open* or *blocked*** is not a decision and gets no ADR. Leave it in the tree where its openness is visible.

Give the `design:adr` skill, per decision: the question, the options considered **and why each was rejected**, the chosen path, the rationale from the closure, and any ADR it supersedes. The rejection reasons are not optional padding — they are what makes the record load-bearing later, when someone is weighing the same option again and needs to know it was already ruled out and on what grounds. Then let it work.

For an artifact marked *not yet templated*, write it from the general rules on this page: provenance, lexicon discipline, and a stated completeness test of your own before you start.

## Common shape

Every artifact opens with the same three lines, because a reader needs them before the content:

- **Sourced from:** the design tree of [date/topic], N branches decided.
- **Gaps:** what could not be written from decided branches, or "none".
- **Inference:** how much of this document is marked inference, in one sentence.

Then the artifact's own content. No preamble, no restating the pitch, no summary of the interview. The reader wants the design, not its history.

# Output Artifacts

Read this at Phase 9, before writing anything.

## Where artifacts go

**Nothing here has a hardcoded path.** The destination comes from the project, and Phase 2 already worked it out: whatever its scans found — ADRs, a lexicon, an assumptions record — establishes where this project keeps design documentation. Write the durable artifacts alongside it; write the feature's brief where the project's conventions say the build reads it (see *Which artifacts this design needs*).

If the scans found nothing and no documentation directory is obvious, ask. Once, in one line, **with a concrete suggestion** — one that fits what the repo actually looks like, its ecosystem's convention or a `docs/` that already exists, rather than a preference of your own. Use the answer for everything in this capture.

Ask at most once per project. After this, the files exist and Phase 2's scan finds them, so the destination is derived rather than asked.

Keep the artifacts together, and keep their names recognizable, because the next interview's scan has to find them.

## Provenance

Artifacts need detail the design tree does not always carry. The tree records decisions; a functional spec records behavior, a data model records constraints, acceptance criteria record cases. Some of that was decided in the interview. Some of it will be you filling gaps.

Both are acceptable. Only one is acceptable *silently*.

- A statement tracing to a branch closed **decided** is written plainly.
- A statement you inferred is **marked as inference, inline, with what it was inferred from.** Not collected in a footnote at the end where it reads as afterthought.
- A statement that would resolve a branch closed **deferred**, **blocked**, or **stable-open** is not written at all. Those are open on purpose, and quietly closing one in prose destroys the reason they were left open.

Never let the two look alike. A document where agreed decisions and plausible invention are typographically identical gets implemented as though all of it was agreed.

## Capture is a completeness check

Anything an artifact needs that the tree doesn't have is a gap in the interview, not a gap in your writing. Treat it that way.

When a section can't be written from decided branches:

1. Name the branches that are missing, or that closed too loosely to write from.
2. Offer to reopen them. This is a normal continuation of Phase 5 and the four locks still apply.
3. Write the section on marked inference only if the user declines.

Reaching the end of capture with no gaps to report is real evidence the interview was thorough. Reaching it having invented a third of the content and said nothing is the failure this phase exists to prevent. **Report the gap count even when it is zero.**

## Vocabulary

Every artifact uses the lexicon, and only the lexicon, for anything the lexicon names. Artifacts diverging on terminology is the specific failure the lexicon exists to prevent, and it shows up here first — the data model calling something a `member` while the contract calls it a `user` is how two correct-looking documents produce two different systems.

A term the artifacts need that isn't in the lexicon is a gap like any other. Surface it; don't quietly coin one.

**Write the lexicon back.** Whenever capture runs, the consolidated lexicon is written back to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above if there wasn't one. This is unconditional and it is not optional: the artifacts are written in this vocabulary, so a reader without the lexicon has documents whose terms mean whatever they assume. It is also what the next interview ingests. Show which entries are new and which changed before writing. An inherited entry changes only where this design changed what the word means.

## Assumptions and tracker candidates

**Write the assumptions record back**, to where it was ingested from, or to the destination established above. Unconditional, like the lexicon, and for the same reason: it is not a deliverable, it is what the next interview reads, and what a review of the build checks its platform assumptions against.

It holds the assumptions still standing, each with a stable id, the assumption in one line, the subject area, and **how you would know it stopped holding** — an assumption recorded without that is decoration; with it, a later interview can actually check — plus the facts the project has measured that would cost time to rediscover. Remove an assumption the interview invalidated rather than annotating it; if the resolution was a real fork it became an ADR, and that is where the history belongs.

**Branches closed *deferred-later*, *blocked*, or *stable-open* are not written to a file.** They are the next design questions, and a file of them turns into a backlog the tracker already is. Emit them as tracker candidates: one line each with the question, why it is open, and **what would resolve it**, for the user to file. The next interview asks which tracker items touch its work.

## Which artifacts this design needs

**Two outlive the feature: the decision records and the lexicon** (and the assumptions record, above). They are kept in the tree and kept true. Everything else in the tables below is **the feature's brief**: it tells the build and its reviewers what was decided, in the detail the tree does not carry, and it is spent when the feature ships — the code is its own domain model and interface contract, the tests carry the criteria, the project's references carry the behaviour. Write the brief where the project's conventions say the build reads it: on the tracker issue when the project works from one, else in the documentation directory marked as a brief. Do not carry a brief into the next interview as if it described the system; scan the code and the durable three instead.

Four are unconditional:

| Artifact | Template |
|---|---|
| Decision records (ADRs) | the `design:adr` skill — see below |
| Functional specification | `artifacts/functional-spec.md` |
| Edge cases and error handling | `artifacts/edge-cases.md` |
| Acceptance criteria | `artifacts/acceptance-criteria.md` |

The rest are selected by the same conditions check that seeded the tree (`conditions-and-patterns.md`). If the condition held at seeding, the artifact is required now:

| Artifact | Required when | Template |
|---|---|---|
| Interface / contract definitions | *Callers you can't change in lockstep*, or any boundary between components that ship or evolve separately | `artifacts/interface-contract.md` |
| Domain model | *The same concept has more than one shape*, *state outlives a single version*, *holds data that belongs to someone else* | `artifacts/domain-model.md` |
| Non-functional requirements | *It runs inside a constrained envelope*, *someone operates it in production* | not yet templated |

There is deliberately no state-machine artifact. State and lifecycle content is unconditional and lives in the functional spec, which already requires every state, every transition, and every terminal state. A separate artifact would reformat content another artifact owns — a pass-through layer. Where a lifecycle is complex enough to need a diagram, the spec renders it as one.

### Decision records

**Every ADR-worthy decision gets an ADR, always.** Not conditional, not on request, not deferred to the user's judgment at write-up time. Invoke the `design:adr` skill and let it write them — it owns format, house rules, numbering, indexing, and supersession, and none of that is reimplemented here.

A branch that closed *decided* is ADR-worthy when a real fork existed and the decision passes the `design:adr` skill's tests for what gets an ADR. A real fork means the closure recorded it as one, with the alternatives and why each was rejected. Read that line; don't reconstruct it from the rationale. A closure recorded as *no fork* is not an ADR no matter how consequential it feels — nothing was chosen.

Not ADR-worthy: decisions with only one option ever available, choices forced by an existing constraint, anything the design-vs-implementation gate would have deferred, and anything an indexed ADR already covers.

Two cases need care:

- **A decision that contradicts an ADR indexed in Phase 2** is a supersession, not a new record. Say so and hand the `design:adr` skill both — it owns what happens next.
- **A branch that closed *stable-open* or *blocked*** is not a decision and gets no ADR. Leave it in the tree where its openness is visible.

Give the `design:adr` skill, per decision: the question, the options considered **and why each was rejected**, the chosen path, the rationale from the closure, and any ADR it supersedes. The rejection reasons are not optional padding — they are what makes the record load-bearing later, when someone is weighing the same option again and needs to know it was already ruled out and on what grounds. Then let it work.

For an artifact marked *not yet templated*, write it from the general rules on this page: provenance, lexicon discipline, and a stated completeness test of your own before you start.

## Common shape

Every artifact opens with the same three lines, because a reader needs them before the content:

- **Sourced from:** the design tree of [date/topic], N branches decided.
- **Gaps:** what could not be written from decided branches, or "none".
- **Inference:** how much of this document is marked inference, in one sentence.

Then the artifact's own content. No preamble, no restating the pitch, no summary of the interview. The reader wants the design, not its history.

# Edge Cases and Error Handling

## What it's for

What happens when things are empty, absent, duplicated, concurrent, slow, malformed, or broken. Always required.

This artifact has an unusual property: **most of it should already exist.** The ambiguity patterns worked during the interview — directionality, expiry and stuck states, reversal, precedence, identity, cardinality, time, ordering, atomicity, trust boundaries, failure surfacing — and their resolutions land here. If this document is hard to write, the patterns weren't applied during the walk, and the honest response is to say so rather than invent the answers now.

Edge cases are where design interviews believe they closed every branch and didn't, because edges surface during implementation rather than during conversation. Writing this artifact is the last chance to catch that before it's expensive.

## Must contain

**Boundary values**, per operation:

- Zero, empty, absent, null — and whether these are distinct from each other here. They usually are, and conflating them is a defect.
- Exactly one, where one is special.
- Maximum, and what a caller sees on crossing it.
- Unbounded growth, and what reclaims it.

**Malformed and hostile input:** what's rejected, where the rejection happens, what the rejecting layer discloses.

**Concurrency:** simultaneous actors on the same thing. What's ordered, what conflicts, how conflicts resolve, what the loser observes.

**Partial failure**, walked seam by seam. For an operation with several effects, fail it at each seam in turn and state what's left behind — and whether that residue is a state the rest of the design knows how to handle. This is the section most often skipped and most often needed.

**Time-related edges:** timeouts, clock skew, expiry boundaries, retries racing the original request, work that outlives the process that started it.

**Stuck states:** anything that can sit unfinished. What breaks it, who can break it, whether it's visibly stuck or looks normal.

**The error inventory.** Every failure mode, and for each: who finds out, through which channel, what they can do about it, and whether the system recovers on its own. A failure nobody learns about needs to be listed as such — silent failure is a design choice and belongs on the record as one.

## Completeness test

**For every operation in the functional spec, this document says what happens when it is given nothing, given too much, given garbage, run twice at once, and interrupted halfway.**

Five questions, every operation. Anything not answerable is a gap to report, not a case to invent.

## Common failures

- **Inventing the answers at write-up time.** These are design decisions, and deciding them here means deciding them alone. If the interview didn't settle it, report the gap.
- **Listing errors without saying who sees them.** An error inventory that omits the audience and channel isn't actionable.
- **Treating "it returns an error" as an answer.** Which error, to whom, retryable or not, and what recovers.
- **Skipping partial failure because the happy path is atomic.** Almost nothing is atomic all the way through. Find the seams.
- **Conflating empty with absent.** Different conditions, usually different correct behavior.

2	
3	## What it's for
4	
5	What the system does, stated precisely enough to implement without asking follow-up questions. This is where "we decided X" becomes "when the user does Y, here is exactly what happens."
6	
7	Always required. It is the artifact the others hang off.

10	
11	Behavior, not structure and not mechanism. *What* happens, under what conditions, in what order, with what result. 12

14	
15	**Scope and non-goals**, both explicit. The non-goals come from branches closed *out-of-scope* and *deferred-later*, with their stated reasons. 16	
17	**The behavior itself**, organized by what the system does rather than by what module does it. For each behavior:
18	
19	- The triggering condition — who or what initiates it, and when.
20	- The preconditions that must hold, and what happens when they don't.
21	- The rules applied, stated so that two readers compute the same result. Where multiple rules can apply to one case, the precedence order, explicitly. "Whichever is more restrictive" is a valid rule and must be named as one.
22	- The observable result — what changed, what the initiator sees, what anyone else sees.
23	- The side effects, and when they fire relative to the primary result: at request, after commit, on a delay. Whether each is durable or best-effort.
24	
25	**State and lifecycle**, wherever an entity moves through states. Every state, every legal transition, what causes each, and which states are terminal. A state with no documented exit is a bug in the design, not a gap in the writing — report it.
26	
27	  When the lifecycle is complex — many states, guarded transitions, transitions that depend on more than the current state — render this section as a table or a diagram rather than prose. That is a presentation choice inside this artifact, not a reason to split it into a separate one.
28	
29	**Rules, in one place.** Business rules scattered through behavior descriptions get implemented three different ways. Where a rule governs more than one behavior, state it once, name it, and reference it.
30

32	
33	**A reader can determine the system's response to any input the spec claims to cover, without inference and without asking you.**

36

38	
39	- **Describing the happy path as though it were the behavior.** The failure and edge behavior lives in its own artifact, but the spec must be complete for the cases it does cover, and must point at the edge-case artifact rather than pretending the edges don't exist.
40	- **Stating rules with unstated precedence.** Two rules that can both apply and no ordering is one of the highest-yield defects to catch here.
41	- **Restating decisions instead of specifying behavior.** "We decided to use optimistic updates" is a tree entry. "When the request fails, the local change reverts and the prior value is restored" is a spec.
42	- **Leaving a state with no exit.** Anything that can be entered and not left is a stuck state; the interview's expiry pattern should have caught it, and if it didn't, that's a branch to reopen.
43	- **Silently resolving a deferred branch.** If the tree deferred it, the spec says it's deferred. Writing behavior for it makes the deferral invisible.

If this document is hard to write, the patterns weren't applied during the walk, and the honest response is to say so rather than invent the answers now.

Edge cases are where design interviews believe they closed every branch and didn't, because edges surface during implementation rather than during conversation. Writing this artifact is the last chance to catch that before it's expensive.

## Must contain

**Boundary values**, per operation:

- Zero, empty, absent, null — and whether these are distinct from each other here. They usually are, and conflating them is a defect.
- Exactly one, where one is special.
- Maximum, and what a caller sees on crossing it.
- Unbounded growth, and what reclaims it.

**Malformed and hostile input:** what's rejected, where the rejection happens, what the rejecting layer discloses.

**Concurrency:** simultaneous actors on the same thing. What's ordered, what conflicts, how conflicts resolve, what the loser observes.

**Partial failure**, walked seam by seam. For an operation with several effects, fail it at each seam in turn and state what's left behind — and whether that residue is a state the rest of the design knows how to handle. This is the section most often skipped and most often needed.

**Time-related edges:** timeouts, clock skew, expiry boundaries, retries racing the original request, work that outlives the process that started it.

**Stuck states:** anything that can sit unfinished. What breaks it, who can break it, whether it's visibly stuck or looks normal.

**The error inventory.** Every failure mode, and for each: who finds out, through which channel, what they can do about it, and whether the system recovers on its own. A failure nobody learns about needs to be listed as such — silent failure is a design choice and belongs on the record as one.

## Completeness test

**For every operation in the functional spec, this document says what happens when it is given nothing, given too much, given garbage, run twice at once, and interrupted halfway.**

Five questions, every operation. Anything not answerable is a gap to report, not a case to invent.

## Common failures

- **Inventing the answers at write-up time.** These are design decisions, and deciding them here means deciding them alone. If the interview didn't settle it, report the gap.
- **Listing errors without saying who sees them.** An error inventory that omits the audience and channel isn't actionable.
- **Treating "it returns an error" as an answer.** Which error, to whom, retryable or not, and what recovers.
- **Skipping partial failure because the happy path is atomic.** Almost nothing is atomic all the way through. Find the seams.
- **Conflating empty with absent.** Different conditions, usually different correct behavior.
# Acceptance Criteria

## What it's for

The sharpest available test of whether the design is complete and whether an implementation is faithful to it. Always required, and written last, because it is the proof of everything above it.

The claim it makes concrete: **if test cases can be written from the design alone, the design is done. If they can't, there's a gap.** That makes this artifact a measuring instrument, not just a deliverable — its failures are more informative than its successes.

## Must contain

**A case per behavior in the functional spec**, in given / when / then form or any form that names preconditions, action, and expected observable result. Vague expectations defeat the purpose: "the request succeeds" is not a criterion; "the record exists with status `accepted` and the caller receives its identifier" is.

**A case per entry in the edge-case artifact.** Boundary values, malformed input, concurrency, partial failure, stuck states. These are the criteria that actually catch regressions; the happy-path cases mostly catch typos.

**Observable results only.** A criterion asserting on internal structure — a helper was called, a field is arranged a certain way — tests the implementation rather than the design, and will break on refactors that changed nothing anyone can see. Assert on what a caller, a user, or an operator can observe.

**Explicit non-criteria**, where useful: behavior deliberately unspecified, so that an implementer knows they have latitude rather than guessing at an unstated requirement. Branches that closed *deferred-implementation* are exactly this, and naming them here is what makes that terminal state useful downstream.

## Completeness test

Applied to itself, and to everything upstream:

- **Every decided branch is represented by at least one case.** A decision with no criterion is a decision nobody will check.
- **Every case traces to something decided.** A criterion you couldn't source is a requirement invented at write-up time; mark it as inference or drop it.
- **No case requires reading the tree to understand.** These are for someone implementing from the documents, who does not have the conversation.

## Common failures

- **Softening a criterion because the design didn't settle it.** This is the failure that matters most. Vagueness here is where an unclosed branch gets laundered into a document that looks finished. Report the gap instead; that is the entire value of writing this artifact.
- **Only happy paths.** The edge-case criteria are the ones worth having.
- **Asserting on internals.** Tests the code, not the design.
- **One giant case per feature.** A case that checks eleven things tells you nothing useful when it fails.
- **Criteria that restate the spec sentence.** If it isn't checkable, it isn't a criterion.

# Plan: CSV export of all orders

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1: Accounting's importer accepts RFC 4180 quoting. Stops holding when an import rejects a quoted field.

**Branches** (all decided; closed by the requester unless marked)
1. **Scope and non-goals.** `python3 -m orders export --csv <path>` writes every order in the book to a file. Non-goals: filtering, other formats, stdout. Fork: stdout or a file → a file, because accounting imports files.
2. **Consumer.** Accounting's importer reads standard UTF-8 CSV, comma-separated, with a header row. No fork.
3. **Columns and order.** `id,customer,total,placed_on`, rows in `list` order (`load_orders`: placed_on, then id). No fork.
4. **Quoting and encoding.** RFC 4180 quoting through Python's `csv` module (minimal quoting, embedded `"` doubled, CRLF row ends); UTF-8 without a BOM. Fork: joining fields by hand, rejected because `Berg, Hanna` would split.
5. **Money and dates.** Totals keep two decimals (`89.50`, and a stored `"89.5"` is written as `89.50`); dates stay ISO (`2026-09-03`). No fork.
6. **Errors.** `export` without `--csv` exits non-zero (argparse, exit 2) with a usage message on stderr. An unwritable path exits 1 with the OS error on stderr and no traceback. No fork.

8. **Testing.** `unittest` cases in `tests/test_export.py`, run with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.
9. **Existing file at `<path>`.** *Closed by me as a suggestion:* overwrite it, as shell redirection would. No fork offered.
10. **Empty book.** *Closed by me as a suggestion:* write the header row only, exit 0.

# Plan: CSV export of all orders

Repo: ordersdesk, base `main` @ ea4086f.

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1: Accounting's importer accepts the RFC 4180 CSV the requester chose (branch 4); nobody has run an import yet. Stops holding when: an import rejects a quoted field or a CRLF row end. *Untested.*

**Branches**
1. Scope and non-goals: decided (requester). `python3 -m orders export --csv <path>` writes every order to a file and is listed in `--help`. Non-goals: filtering, other formats, CSV on stdout. Fork: stdout vs a file → a file; accounting imports files.
2. Consumer: decided (requester). Accounting's importer; standard UTF-8 CSV, comma-separated, header row. No fork.
3. Columns and order: decided (me, suggestion; **requester to confirm**). Header `id,customer,total,placed_on` (the `Order` field names); rows in `list` order. No fork.
4. Quoting and encoding: decided (requester). RFC 4180 via Python's `csv` default dialect (minimal quoting, `"` doubled, CRLF row ends); file opened `encoding="utf-8"`, `newline=""`, no BOM. Fork: hand-joined fields, rejected because `Berg, Hanna` would split.
5. Money and dates: decided (requester). Totals written with exactly two decimals (`89.50`, `7.5` → `7.50`); dates ISO. No fork.
6. Errors and output: decided (me, suggestion). Missing `--csv` → argparse usage error, exit 2, stderr names `--csv`. Unwritable path (missing directory, path is a directory, no permission) → exit 1, one line `orders: error: <OS error>` on stderr, no traceback. Success prints nothing. No fork.
7. What must not change: decided (requester). `orders list` output, `data/orders.json`, existing tests.
8. Testing: decided (me). `unittest` in `tests/test_export.py`, all file output under a temporary directory; run by `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.
9. Edge outcomes: decided (me, suggestion; **requester to confirm**). Empty book → header only; existing file at `<path>` → overwritten.
10. Totals with more than two decimals: **open, requester to choose.** My suggestion: refuse the export (exit 1, name the order id) rather than round money silently. Alternative: round half-up.
11. Module shape: decided (me). New `orders/export.py` with `write_csv(orders, path)`; `__main__.py` only adds the subcommand, like `list` uses `store`. No fork.
12. Docs: decided (me). README gains the `export` line.

**Lexicon delta:** none. **ADR-worthy:** branch 4. Counts: 9 decided, 2 awaiting confirmation (3, 9), 1 open (10).

## 2. Brief
- **Sourced from:** design tree of 2026-10-20, CSV export.
- **Gaps:** branch 10 open; branches 3 and 9 unconfirmed.
- **Inference:** branches 3, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 are my suggestions.

### Functional spec
- `export --csv <path>` calls `load_orders()` and `write_csv()` [1][11].
- UTF-8, no BOM, `newline=""`, `csv.writer` default dialect [4].
- Header `id,customer,total,placed_on`, then one row per order in `load_orders()` order [3].
- `total` with exactly two decimals; `placed_on` ISO [5]; branch 10 governs >2 decimals.
- Exit 0, empty stdout on success [6].

### Edge cases
- E1 [6] no `--csv` → exit 2, stderr contains `the following arguments are required: --csv`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.ExportCliTest.test_missing_csv_is_usage_error`
- E2 [6] path in a missing directory, or path that is a directory → exit 1, stderr starts `orders: error:`, no `Traceback`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.ExportCliTest.test_unwritable_path_reports_os_error`
- E3 [9] empty book → header only. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.WriteCsvTest.test_empty_book_writes_header_only`
- E4 [9] existing file → overwritten. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.WriteCsvTest.test_existing_file_is_overwritten`
- E5 [5] total `7.5` → `7.50`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.WriteCsvTest.test_total_padded_to_two_decimals`
- E6 [10] total `7.505` → per branch 10. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.WriteCsvTest.test_total_with_more_than_two_decimals`

### Acceptance criteria
- AC1 [1][3] exit 0, empty stdout, file = header + ids 1001–1005 in order. Check: `…ExportCliTest.test_writes_every_order_in_list_order`
- AC2 [4] `"Berg, Hanna"` quoted, CRLF row ends, `csv.reader` reads 6 rows of 4 fields. Check: `…ExportCliTest.test_rfc4180_quoting`
- AC3 [4] bytes start `id,`; decode UTF-8 to `Åkesson & Dotter`, `Sjöberg Trading`; holds with `PYTHONIOENCODING`/`LC_ALL=C` set in the subprocess (catches a missing `encoding=`). Check: `…ExportCliTest.test_utf8_without_bom`
- AC4 [5] row `1002,Norrlands Café,89.50,2026-09-03`. Check: `…ExportCliTest.test_money_and_dates`
- AC5 [1] `--help` lists `export`. Check: `…ExportCliTest.test_help_lists_export`
- AC6 [12] README documents `export --csv`. Check: `grep -q 'orders export --csv' README.md`

### Guardrails
- G1 [7] `list` output unchanged: test compares `main(["list"])` stdout to the 5 lines hard-coded from base output. Check: `…GuardrailTest.test_list_output_unchanged`
- G2 [7] an export that succeeds (exit 0, 6-line file) leaves `data/orders.json`'s sha256 unchanged. Check: `…GuardrailTest.test_export_leaves_order_book_untouched`. (At base it fails on the exit-0 precondition; that's expected for a guardrail coupled to the feature. G1 and G3 are the pure guardrails.)
- G3 [7] `python3 -m unittest tests.test_store` passes.

## 3. Slices
| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 CSV export | ordersdesk | main @ ea4086f | single vertical | `feat/orders-csv-export` → main |

One slice: additive and small; a split would ship a writer with no caller.

## 4. Capture (first commit of S1)
- ADR-0001 "Export orders as RFC 4180 CSV, UTF-8 without BOM" [4] → `docs/adr/` (suggested; repo has no docs).
- Lexicon: no change.
- Assumptions: `docs/assumptions.md` with A1 [4].

# Plan: CSV export of all orders

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1: Accounting's importer accepts RFC 4180 quoting. Stops holding when an import rejects a quoted field.

**Branches** (closed by the requester unless marked *suggestion*)
1. **Scope and non-goals.** `python3 -m orders export --csv <path>` writes every order in the book to a file. Non-goals: filtering, other formats, stdout, and *(suggestion)* spreadsheet formula escaping, because the reader is an importer, not a spreadsheet. `--csv -` writes a file named `-`. Fork: stdout or a file → a file.
2. **Consumer.** Accounting's importer: standard UTF-8 CSV, comma-separated, with a header row. No fork.
3. **Columns and order.** `id,customer,total,placed_on`, rows in `list` order (placed_on, then id). No fork.
4. **Quoting and encoding.** RFC 4180 via Python's `csv` module (minimal quoting, embedded `"` doubled, CRLF row ends), with the file opened `newline=""`, explicitly UTF-8 with no BOM. Fork: joining fields by hand, rejected because `Berg, Hanna` would split.
5. **Money and dates.** Totals keep two decimals (`89.50`, and a stored `89.5` or `15` is padded). Dates are ISO. *(suggestion)* A total with more than two decimals is refused (exit 1, message naming the order id) rather than rounded, because an export that quietly changes money is worse than one that stops.
6. **Errors.** `export` without `--csv` exits 2 with argparse usage on stderr. An unwritable path exits 1 with the OS error on stderr and no traceback. *(suggestion)* The message reads `orders: <error>`. A missing order book is handled the same way (exit 1). Malformed JSON behaves as it does for `list` today.
7. **What must not change.** `orders list` output and `data/orders.json`; the existing tests keep passing.
8. **Testing.** `unittest` in `tests/test_export.py` and `tests/test_list.py`, run by `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`. CLI behaviour is tested by calling `main()` with `orders.__main__.load_orders` patched to read a temporary book. Error paths and encoding run `python3 -m orders` as a subprocess.
9. **Existing file at `<path>`.** *(suggestion)* It is replaced.
10. **Empty book.** *(suggestion)* The file gets the header row only, and the command exits 0.
11. **A write that fails partway.** *(suggestion)* The export writes a temporary file beside `<path>`, then `os.replace`s it in. On failure the previous file stays intact and no temporary file is left behind. Fork: write in place, rejected because accounting could import a half-written file.

**Lexicon delta:** none. **ADR-worthy:** branches 4 and 11.

**Shape.** `orders/export.py` has `write_csv(orders, path)`. It owns columns, dialect, encoding, money format and the atomic replace, and raises `ValueError` for a total with more than two decimals. `__main__.py` gains an `export` subparser with a required `--csv`. It calls `write_csv(load_orders(), args.csv)` and maps `OSError`/`ValueError` to `orders: <error>` on stderr and a return of 1.

2. **Consumer.** Accounting's importer reads standard UTF-8 CSV, comma-separated, with a header row. No fork.
3. **Columns and order.** `id,customer,total,placed_on`, rows in `list` order (`load_orders`: placed_on, then id). No fork.
4. **Quoting and encoding.** RFC 4180 quoting through Python's `csv` module (minimal quoting, embedded `"` doubled, CRLF row ends); UTF-8 without a BOM. Fork: joining fields by hand, rejected because `Berg, Hanna` would split.
5. **Money and dates.** Totals keep two decimals (`89.50`, and a stored `"89.5"` is written as `89.50`); dates stay ISO (`2026-09-03`). No fork.
6. **Errors.** `export` without `--csv` exits non-zero (argparse, exit 2) with a usage message on stderr. An unwritable path exits 1 with the OS error on stderr and no traceback. No fork.

9. **Existing file at `<path>`.** *Closed by me as a suggestion:* overwrite it, as shell redirection would. No fork offered.
10. **Empty book.** *Closed by me as a suggestion:* write the header row only, exit 0.

# Plan: CSV export of all orders

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1 — Accounting's importer accepts RFC 4180 quoting. Stops holding when: an import rejects a quoted field.

**Branches**
1. **Scope and non-goals** — decided (requester). `python3 -m orders export --csv <path>` writes every order in the book to a file and prints nothing to stdout (suggested by Claude). Non-goals: filtering, other formats, stdout. Fork: stdout vs a file → a file; accounting imports files.
2. **Consumer** — decided (requester). Accounting's importer reads standard UTF-8 CSV, comma-separated, with a header row. No fork.
3. **Columns and order** — decided (requester). `id,customer,total,placed_on`, rows in `list` order (oldest first, then id), because both read the book through `load_orders`. No fork.
4. **Quoting and encoding** — decided (requester). RFC 4180 quoting through Python's `csv` module: fields are quoted only when needed, `"` is doubled, and rows end in CRLF. UTF-8 without a byte-order mark, written explicitly rather than from the locale. Fork: joining fields by hand, rejected because `Berg, Hanna` would split. Formula-injection escaping (cells starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`) is a non-goal (suggested by Claude): the reader is an importer, not a spreadsheet.
5. **Money and dates** — decided (requester). Totals always have two decimals (`89.50`); a stored `89.5` is written `89.50`. Rounding beyond two decimals uses Decimal's default half-even (suggested by Claude; the book stores two). Dates are ISO (`2026-09-03`). No fork.
6. **Errors** — decided (requester); the exact surface is suggested by Claude. `export` without `--csv` gives argparse's usage error, exit 2. When the file can't be opened or written (missing directory, permission denied, the path is a directory), stderr gets `orders: error: <OS error>`, exit 1, no traceback. A missing or malformed `data/orders.json` behaves exactly as it does for `list` today (out of scope). No fork.
7. **What must not change** — decided (requester). `orders list` output and `data/orders.json` stay as they are, and the existing tests keep passing.
8. **Testing** — decided (requester). `unittest` cases in `tests/test_export.py`, run with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`. Behaviour on the real book runs as a subprocess of `python3 -m orders`. Fixture books are swapped in by patching `orders.__main__.load_orders` to `load_orders(fixture)`, so the store's real sorting still applies (suggested by Claude).
9. **Edge inputs** — decided (Claude, as a suggestion; **pending your confirmation**). An empty book writes the header row only. An existing file at `<path>` is overwritten. A write that fails halfway may leave a partial file, with no atomic rename, because the command is re-run by hand. No fork.

**Lexicon delta:** none. The project has no lexicon; "order", "order book" and "total" are used as in the code.

**Counts:** 9 branches. 8 decided by the requester, of which 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 carry details suggested by Claude, marked inline. Branch 9 is suggested by Claude and pending. 0 open.

## 2. Brief

- **Sourced from:** the design tree of 2026-10-20, CSV export. 9 branches.
- **Gaps:** branch 9 and the Claude-suggested details in branches 1, 4, 5, 6 and 8 await the requester's confirmation.
- **Inference:** limited to the items marked "suggested by Claude" in the tree.

### Functional spec
- **Scope:** `python3 -m orders export --csv <path>` [1]. Non-goals: filtering, other formats, stdout, formula escaping, book-loading errors [1][4][6].
- **Trigger:** the operator runs the command [1].
- **Rules:** the first row is `id,customer,total,placed_on`. Then one row per order, in the order `orders list` prints them [3]. Quoting is RFC 4180 via `csv`, with CRLF row endings [4]. Encoding is UTF-8 with no BOM, independent of locale [4]. Totals are quantized to two decimals; `placed_on` is ISO 8601 [5].
- **Result:** `<path>` is created or overwritten [9]. Exit 0, empty stdout [1]. `data/orders.json` is only read [7].

### Edge cases
- Empty book → header row only [9].
- `--csv` missing → usage error, exit 2 [6].
- `<path>` can't be opened (missing directory, permission denied, is a directory) → `orders: error: <OS error>`, exit 1, no traceback [6].
- Customer containing a comma, `"` or non-ASCII → quoted as RFC 4180 requires, and round-trips through `csv.reader` [4].
- Total stored as `89.5` → `89.50` [5].
- Existing file longer than the new output → replaced exactly [9].
- Interrupted write → partial file may remain [9].
- Non-criteria: book-loading errors [6], formula escaping [4].

### Acceptance criteria
Checks run from the repo root. `tests.test_export` holds `RealBookTest`, which runs a subprocess on `data/orders.json`, and `FixtureBookTest`, which patches the loader to a fixture.

- **AC1 [1][3]** On the real book, `export --csv out.csv` exits 0 with empty stdout. The file is the header plus 5 rows with ids 1001–1005. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.RealBookTest.test_writes_header_and_every_order`
- **AC2 [3]** Fixture book stored out of order, with a same-date pair in reverse id order: export's id column equals the ids `list` prints from the same fixture, and equals the sorted order. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.FixtureBookTest.test_rows_follow_list_order`
- **AC3 [4]** Fixture customers are `Berg, Hanna` and `Café "Nord"`. The raw file contains `"Berg, Hanna"` and `"Café ""Nord"""`, every row ends `\r\n`, and `csv.reader` reads both names back unchanged. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.FixtureBookTest.test_quotes_per_rfc4180`
- **AC4 [2][4]** On the real book, under `PYTHONUTF8=0 LC_ALL=C`: the bytes don't start with `EF BB BF`, and they decode as UTF-8 containing `Åkesson & Dotter`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.RealBookTest.test_utf8_without_bom_regardless_of_locale`
- **AC5 [5]** On the real book, the row for 1002 is exactly `1002,Norrlands Café,89.50,2026-09-03`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.RealBookTest.test_money_and_dates`
- **EC1 [6]** `export` with no `--csv` exits 2. stderr contains `the following arguments are required: --csv` and not `invalid choice`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.RealBookTest.test_missing_csv_is_usage_error`
- **EC2 [6]** `--csv <tmp>/missing/out.csv`, a `--csv` that is a directory, and (when not root) one inside a `0o500` directory: each exits 1, stderr starts `orders: error:` with the OS message, and there's no `Traceback`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.RealBookTest.test_unwritable_path_reports_os_error`
- **EC3 [9]** Empty fixture book → the file is exactly `id,customer,total,placed_on\r\n`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.FixtureBookTest.test_empty_book_writes_header_only`
- **EC4 [5]** A fixture order with total `"89.5"` → its row has `89.50`. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.FixtureBookTest.test_one_decimal_total_gets_two`
- **EC5 [9]** `<path>` pre-filled with 4 KiB of `STALE` → after export, the file equals the expected output byte for byte. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.RealBookTest.test_overwrites_existing_file`
- **EC6 [9]** Interrupted write leaves a partial file. Check: judged (accepted, untested).

### Guardrails
- **G1 [7]** `orders list` prints the same at base and head. Check: `diff <(cd "$BASE_WT" && python3 -m orders list) <(python3 -m orders list)`, where `$BASE_WT` is a worktree of `main`.
- **G2 [7]** `data/orders.json` is unchanged in git and by running export. Check: `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.RealBookTest.test_does_not_touch_order_book` (SHA-256 and mtime of the book before and after the CLI run), then `git diff --exit-code main -- data/orders.json` after the full suite.
- **G3 [7][8]** The whole suite passes. Check: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## 3. Slices

| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 CSV export | ordersdesk | `main` (ea4086f) | `feat/orders-csv-export` → `main` | — (opened after approval) |

One slice, cut vertically. It's a purely additive leaf feature: a new module and subcommand, with no existing behaviour changed. Splitting it further would ship a writer nothing calls.

## 4. Capture
- ADR-0001 "Export orders as RFC 4180 CSV, UTF-8 without BOM" [4], in `docs/adr/` (suggested; the repo has no docs directory yet).
- Lexicon: no change. Nothing is coined, so no lexicon file is created.
- Assumptions: add A1 [4] to `docs/assumptions.md` (new).

## 5. Progress
- [x] Intake
- [x] Designing
- [ ] Planning
- [ ] Building slices
- [ ] Proving changes
- [ ] Shipping PRs

# Plan: CSV export of all orders

Repo: ordersdesk, base `main` @ `ea4086f`. Python 3.15, stdlib only.

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- A1 [2][4] — Accounting's importer accepts comma-delimited RFC 4180 CSV: quoted fields (including quoted line breaks), decimal point, CRLF after every row including the last. Stops holding when: an import rejects or mis-splits a file.
- A2 [4] — Accounting reads the file only through its importer, never by opening it in a spreadsheet. Stops holding when: someone opens the export in Excel/Numbers.

**Branches**
1. **Scope and non-goals** — decided (requester). `python3 -m orders export --csv <path>` writes every order in the book to a file. Non-goals: filtering, other formats, stdout, `-` meaning stdout. Fork: stdout vs file → file.
2. **Consumer** — decided (requester). Accounting's importer; standard UTF-8 CSV, comma-separated, header row. No fork.
3. **Columns and order** — decided (requester). `id,customer,total,placed_on`, rows in `list` order. No fork. *Empty book → header only* — me, suggestion.
4. **Quoting and encoding** — decided (requester). RFC 4180 via `csv`; UTF-8, no BOM. Fork: hand-joined fields, rejected (`Berg, Hanna` would split). *CRLF row endings; doubled embedded quotes; line breaks in a name stay, quoted; no formula-injection escaping (A2)* — me, suggestion.
5. **Money and dates** — decided (requester). Totals always two decimals (`89.5` → `89.50`); dates ISO. *A total with more than two decimals refuses the export: exit 1, naming the order id, no file written. Negative totals are written with a leading minus (`-15.00`)* — me, suggestion; **open to you, see Q1**.
6. **Errors** — decided (requester). Missing `--csv` → exit 2, argparse usage. Unwritable path → exit 1, `orders: error: <OS error>` on stderr, no traceback. *Covers missing parent (not created) and a directory as target* — me, suggestion.
7. **What must not change** — decided (requester). `orders list` output, `data/orders.json`, existing tests.
8. **Testing** — decided (requester), amended by me: `tests/test_export.py` for the feature; G1's golden test in `tests/test_list_output.py`.
9. **Existing file at path** — me, suggestion. Replaced entirely. Not atomic; a mid-write failure may leave a partial file, signalled by exit 1.
10. **Docs and records** — me, suggestion. README gains an `export` line; ADRs in `docs/adr/`, assumptions in `docs/assumptions.md`.
11. **Writer interface** — me, suggestion. `orders/export.py` exposes `write_csv(orders, path)`; `__main__` loads the book and calls it. Edge cases needing constructed orders test it directly; everything else goes through the CLI.

**Lexicon delta:** none.

## 2. Brief
- **Sourced from:** design tree 2026-10-20, 8 branches decided by requester, 3 closed by me as suggestion. **Gaps:** Q1 pending. **Inference:** the "suggestion" items only.

The plan is ready for your approval. An independent reviewer went through it and found 15 problems; I've fixed them below. Nothing is written to the repo yet. There's no plan mode in this session, so the plan lives only in this reply and in `$TMPDIR/delivering-pitches/plan.md`, and it won't survive a context clear.

# Plan: CSV export of all orders

**Repo:** ordersdesk. It branches from `main` at `ea4086f`, has one passing test, and uses only the standard library.

## 1. Design

**Assumptions**
- **A1** [2][4]: Accounting's importer accepts standard CSV (RFC 4180). That means comma-delimited, quoted fields (line breaks inside quotes included), a decimal point, and CRLF at the end of every row including the last. *We'd know it stopped holding when* an import rejects a file or splits a row wrongly.
- **A2** [4]: Accounting only reads the file through its importer and never opens it in a spreadsheet. *We'd know it stopped holding when* someone opens the export in Excel or Numbers.

**Branches.** "Me" means I closed the choice as a suggestion.

1. **Scope:** decided by you. `export --csv <path>` writes every order to a file. Not included: filtering, other formats, writing to stdout, or `-` meaning stdout.
2. **Consumer:** decided by you. Accounting's importer reads UTF-8 CSV, comma-separated, with a header row.
3. **Columns and order:** decided by you. `id,customer,total,placed_on`, in `list` order. *If there are no orders, the file has just the header row* (me).
4. **Quoting and encoding:** decided by you. Standard quoting through Python's `csv` module, UTF-8 with no byte-order mark. Joining fields by hand was rejected because `Berg, Hanna` would split. *Also from me:*
   - rows end in CRLF;
   - a double quote inside a field is written twice;
   - a line break inside a name is kept inside quotes;
   - names starting with `=` are not escaped against spreadsheet formulas (relies on A2).
5. **Money and dates:** decided by you. Totals always have two decimals (`89.5` → `89.50`) and dates stay ISO. *If a total has more than two decimals, the export refuses: exit 1, naming the order, and no file is written. Negative totals are written as `-15.00`.* This part is from me, and it's **Q1** below.
6. **Errors:** decided by you. Leaving out `--csv` exits with code 2 and the usage message. A path that can't be written exits with code 1 and prints `orders: error: <OS error>` without a traceback. *That covers a missing parent folder, which isn't created, and a path that is a folder* (me).
7. **What must not change:** decided by you. `orders list` output, `data/orders.json` and the existing tests.
8. **Testing:** decided by you, plus one change from me. The new tests go in `tests/test_export.py`, and the test for G1 below goes in `tests/test_list_output.py`.
9. **Existing file at the path:** me. It's replaced entirely. The write isn't atomic: if it fails halfway, it can leave a partial file, and the exit code 1 signals that.
10. **Docs:** me. The README gets an `export` line. ADRs go in `docs/adr/` and assumptions in `docs/assumptions.md`, since the repo has no docs folder yet.
11. **Writer:** me. `orders/export.py` provides `write_csv(orders, path)`. Edge cases that need made-up orders call it directly; everything else goes through the command line.

**Lexicon:** no change.

## 2. Brief
- **Behaviour:** the command writes every order in `list` order: the header, then one row per order, using the quoting, encoding and number rules above. It exits 0 and prints nothing.
- **Gaps:** Q1 is still open.

**Acceptance criteria.** Each check runs `python3 -m unittest tests.test_export.ExportTest.<name>`.

| id | branch | what must be true | test name |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC1 | [1][3] | Exits 0, prints nothing, writes the header then 1001–1005 in order | `test_writes_header_and_every_order_in_list_order` |
| AC2 | [4] | The line reads `1004,"Berg, Hanna",15.00,2026-09-08` | `test_quotes_customer_with_comma` |
| AC3 | [4] | No byte-order mark; `Åkesson & Dotter` is UTF-8, even with `PYTHONUTF8=0 LC_ALL=C` set | `test_utf8_without_bom` |
| AC4 | [5] | The lines for 1001 and 1002 read exactly as expected (`1250.00`, `89.50`) | `test_total_two_decimals_and_iso_date` |
| AC5 | [6] | Exits 2 and says `the following arguments are required: --csv` | `test_missing_csv_flag_is_usage_error` |
| AC6 | [6] | Missing parent folder: exits 1 with `orders: error:` and the OS message, no traceback, folder not created | `test_missing_parent_reports_os_error` |
| AC7 | [6] | Path is a folder: exits 1 with `orders: error:`, no traceback | `test_directory_target_reports_os_error` |

**Edge cases**

| id | branch | case | expected | test name |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | [3] | No orders | Exactly `id,customer,total,placed_on\r\n` | `test_empty_book_writes_header_only` |
| E2 | [9] | A longer file already exists | Fully replaced | `test_overwrites_existing_file` |
| E3 | [5] | Total `89.5` | `89.50` | `test_pads_total_to_two_decimals` |
| E4 | [4] | Customer `Say "Hi" AB` | `"Say ""Hi"" AB"` | `test_doubles_embedded_quotes` |
| E5 | [4] | Shipped data | Exact bytes: every row ends `\r\n`, never `\r\r` | `test_rows_end_with_crlf` |
| E6 | [5] | Total `12.345` | Refused, names the order, no file *(Q1)* | `test_rejects_total_with_more_than_two_decimals` |
| E7 | [5] | Total `-15` | `-15.00` *(Q1)* | `test_writes_negative_total` |

I'll check two things by reading rather than with a test: the partial file after a failed write, and the README line.

**Guardrails.** For each one I'll make a one-line change that should break it and confirm the check fails.

| id | branch | must stay true | check | breaking change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | [7] | `orders list` prints exactly what `ea4086f` prints | `python3 -m unittest tests.test_list_output` | change the total's width `>10` to `>11` |
| G2 | [7] | `data/orders.json` is unchanged | `git diff --exit-code ea4086f -- data/orders.json` | append a newline to the file |
| G3 | [7] | The existing store test passes | `python3 -m unittest tests.test_store` | `reverse=True` in `load_orders` |

## 3. Slices
| Slice | Repo | Base | Direction | PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 `feat/orders-csv-export` | ordersdesk | `main` @ `ea4086f` | additive, vertical | #1 → `main` |

It's one slice because the feature is one new command. Shipping the writer and the command separately would leave a module nothing uses.

## 4. Capture
- **ADR-0001** "CSV dialect for the accounting export" [4][5]
- **Lexicon:** no change
- **Assumptions:** a new `docs/assumptions.md` holding A1 [2][4] and A2 [4]

## 5. Progress
- [x] Intake
- [x] Designing
- [ ] Planning
- [ ] Building slices
- [ ] Proving changes
- [ ] Shipping PRs

## What the review changed
- **G3's check didn't catch its own breaking change.** The old one swapped the tiebreak between two orders placed the same day, and the store test has no such orders. It's now `reverse=True`.
- **Line endings:** checking only that rows "end with `\r\n`" would also pass on a doubled `\r\r\n`, so E5 now compares exact bytes.
- **Encoding:** Python 3.15 defaults to UTF-8, so AC3 now runs with UTF-8 mode turned off.
- **AC5** used to pass before the change too, since an unknown command also exits 2. It now checks the exact message.
- **Totals:** AC4 can't catch a missing two-decimal rule, because the shipped data already has two decimals. E3 covers that rule.
- **New checks:** AC1 now also checks that nothing is printed, AC6 checks the folder isn't created, AC7 is new, and E2 now runs through the command line.
- **Gaps closed:** branch 11 and A2 are new, and A1 is wider.
- **Smaller notes I left as non-goals:** there's no currency column, names aren't Unicode-normalized, and `--csv -` writes a file literally named `-`.

## Questions
- **Q1.** What should happen to a total with more than two decimals? I suggest refusing the export (E6) rather than rounding, because the default rounding (to even) turns `12.345` into `12.34` and accounting usually expects `12.35`. And are negative totals (credit notes) possible? If so, should they be `-15.00`?
- **Q2.** Are you OK not escaping names that start with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, given A2?

Do you approve the plan, with your answers to Q1 and Q2?

- delivery:pr: Use when writing a PR body.
- design:adr: House rules and format for Architecture Decision Records. Load before writing, reviewing, superseding, or indexing an ADR in any repo, and when asked to record a decision, write something up as an ADR, add to or reindex a directory of ADRs, or change an ADR's Status. Also load when deciding whether a decision warrants an ADR at all, and when something about a decision already recorded in an ADR has changed, to decide between a superseding ADR and an addendum. NOT for architecture pages on the wiki, RFCs, or design docs that record no decision.
- design:design-interview: Drives a thorough design interview that takes a software engineer from a rough pitch to a complete, gap-free design before code is written. Use this skill whenever the user wants to design new functionality, plan a change to existing code, extend a codebase, or work out the shape of a feature before implementing it. Trigger on phrases like "design X", "help me design", "plan a change to", "before I write code", "let's think through", "I'm planning to add", "I want to build", "how should I structure", and on substantive change descriptions even without an explicit design ask, since pre-implementation is when this skill is most valuable. Produces a complete design tree — every branch closed in a terminal state with its rationale — laid out in context when the interview ends, and on request captures it as functional spec, contracts, edge cases, acceptance criteria, and ADRs.
- design:design-philosophy: Load first, before the first Edit or Write, whenever a request will have you write or change code that adds or changes behaviour — a feature, a bug fix, error handling, a new option, a refactor — however small it looks. Where the new logic lives and what its callers see are structural decisions, and these principles govern them here. Also load before designing or planning a change, and at the start of a design interview, before any branch is seeded. Carries the structural principles that govern how software here is built — complexity as the thing to minimize, deep modules behind small interfaces, information hiding, no pass-through layers, pushing complexity down, considering alternatives before committing, long-term simplicity over short-term speed. Trigger on implement, add, build, extend, refactor, restructure, design, plan. NOT for mechanical edits whose decisions are already made (a typo, a rename, formatting), and NOT for code-level style: formatting, naming conventions, comment mechanics.
- design:lexicon: House rules for a project's lexicon — the domain's ubiquitous language — and the procedure for pruning, consolidating and correcting one that has sprawled. Load before admitting, amending or retiring a lexicon or glossary entry in any repo; when asked to review, audit, prune, consolidate, clean up or correct a lexicon or glossary; and when a lexicon has grown past about thirty entries or its entries describe code rather than meaning. design-interview loads it for the admission tests. NOT for API reference documentation, code doc comments, or user manuals.
- implementation:code-style: Load first, before the first Edit or Write, whenever a request will have you choose or change a name, or write or change a comment or the code it sits in — a rename, even one whose new name is given, a pass over comments or docstrings, a feature, a bug fix, a refactor — however mechanical it looks. A rename is a naming decision, and the comments that name the old thing go stale with it; how a name or a comment reads is decided as it is written, and these principles govern both here. Carries the house rules for names (name it what it is, call it what it does; domain words from the lexicon) and for comments (say what the code cannot: delete what the name, signature and code in view already say, keep what depends on context that lives elsewhere, and shrink a comment that mixes both, clause by clause). Trigger on implement, add, fix, refactor, rename, comment, document, tidy, clean up. NOT for a typo in prose or a formatting change that alters no name and no comment.
- implementation:review-cycle: The pre-PR review cycle: fresh-context reviewers by lens (adversarial, design parity, simplification, platform reality, and lenses the repository adds as skills of its own), then triage, fix, record and re-run. Load when a branch is ready for its pull request, when asked to review your own branch or an issue's work before it goes up, or when the user invokes /review-cycle. NOT for reviewing a pull request someone else opened, and NOT a substitute for running the build and the tests.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a change to Claude's own interface or behaviour, such as a live pane or panel, a band above the prompt, a status line, a toast, a slash command, or a hook on tool calls or prompts. Use to make, change or debug a mod or its hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Load when a branch is ready for its pull request, when asked to review your own branch or an issue's work before it goes up, or when the user invokes /review-cycle. NOT for reviewing a pull request someone else opened, and NOT a substitute for running the build and the tests.

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
